sources.title: David Unaipon (Q939297), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'David Unaipon', description 'Indigenous Australian inventor and writer (1872-1967)', instance of human, born 28 September 1872, died 7 February 1967, citizenship Australia; no Korean label or Korean Wikipedia article. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Philip Jones, 'Unaipon, David (1872-1967)', Australian Dictionary of Biography, volume 12 (Melbourne University Press, 1990), read in full from the online edition. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: preacher, author and inventor; mission-school education and years as a servant to C. B. Young; self-directed reading; a modified shearing handpiece patented by 1909 and nine further patent applications between 1909 and 1944 that lapsed; his obsession with perpetual motion; fifty years travelling south-eastern Australia as a subscription collector for the Aborigines' Friends' Association, lecturing and preaching; his legends compiled from the early 1920s and published under William Ramsay Smith's name without acknowledgment in 1930; evidence to royal commissions in 1913 and 1926 and help to the 1928-29 Bleakley inquiry; his skill with the press; still preaching at 87 and working on his inventions in his nineties. Reference biography, sympathetic but candid about the reputation-building ('black genius', 'Australia's Leonardo') and the limits placed on him.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'David Unaipon' (read in full): Ngarrindjeri inventor, author and advocate; the shearing handpiece that converts circular into straight-line motion, patented by 1909 but later adopted without crediting him apart from one 1910 newspaper article; provisional patents he could not afford to complete; the 1920s-30s newspaper articles and booklets; the manuscript he gathered from 1924 that was sold to William Ramsay Smith and published under Smith's name in 1930, with Unaipon credited as author only in 2001. Short reference article.

Billy Griffiths, essay on David Unaipon's 'Legendary Tales of the Australian Aborigines', Reading Australia (Copyright Agency and AustLit; read in full): historian's account of the 1924-25 collecting tour with an Indigenous translator, the Angus & Robertson contract at two guineas per thousand words, the breakdown of communication in August 1925, Ramsay Smith's purchase of the manuscript and his 1930 edition that removed Unaipon's voice and interpretations, the 2001 restoration by Stephen Muecke and Adam Shoemaker, his provisional patents and boomerang-based helicopter design, and his formal, biblical and classical writing style. Draws on the 2001 edition's introduction and on Jenkin and Jones. Independent scholarly framing; admiring.

Reserve Bank of Australia banknotes site, 'David Unaipon (1872-1967)' people-on-the-banknotes entry (read in full): writer, public speaker and inventor; list of inventions and his inability to obtain financial backing; the 1914 helicopter idea drawn from the boomerang; the 1924-1929 first publications; 1928-29 Bleakley inquiry; 1934 proposals on Aboriginal affairs; 1953 Coronation Medal. Institutional biography written for the banknote; largely follows the ADB.

'Problem of Perpetual Motion: Australian Native's Invention', The Press (Christchurch), 24 July 1919, p. 3, via Papers Past (read in full; a New Zealand reprint of a South Australian Register piece, also reprinted in the Thames Star, 18 August 1919): contemporary description of his work on perpetual motion over many years, his claim to have an appliance harnessing gravitation, his lecturing campaign to raise money for a patent, his statement that he had not demonstrated it in public, and the shearing handpiece patent. Contemporary newspaper report, partly his own account, in the paternalistic tone of the time.

Kym Kropinyeri and Kathy Bowery, 'David Unaipon, inventor', Australian Historical Studies 54(4), 2023 (journal abstract page and first-page excerpt read; the full article was not available): scholarly account of his patent applications, the Protection-era restrictions on Aboriginal inventors, the fate of the 1909 shearing patent set against Cooper Engineering's patent activity, and the pressures from the Chief Protector, politicians, religious groups, museum staff, mission superintendents and police that limited his scientific work and led to poverty. Used only for the framing that his inventing was constrained from outside; no row rests on it.

Australian War Memorial, 'David Unaipon', Forging the Nation: Federation, the First 20 Years (read in full): short profile saying he sought to improve the education of Aboriginal people, wanted Aboriginal culture understood (quoting his wish for 'an enduring record of our customs, beliefs, and imaginings'), represented Aboriginal views at a royal commission in 1913, studied aerodynamics, lodged ten patents, and was often refused accommodation because of his race. Short institutional profile.

Encyclopedia of Australian Science and Innovation (Swinburne University of Technology), 'Unaipon, David (1872-1967)' (read in full): Ngarrindjeri Elder, author and inventor; occupations and career summary; chronology of 1912, 1926 and 1934 appeals; bibliography listing the 1930 Ramsay Smith book as an unacknowledged version of Unaipon's work and the 2006 Miegunyah edition; archival holdings of the manuscript at the Mitchell Library. Reference entry; derived from the ADB.

persistence.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_press1919, src_unaipon_britannica, src_unaipon_rba | 1909-1967 | reference biography, contemporary newspaper, encyclopaedia, institutional biography] He kept working on perpetual motion for decades: the 1919 report says disappointments 'innumerable' did not stop him, the ADB has him still convinced in his nineties that he was close, and he made patent applications over thirty-five years (1909-1944) although they lapsed; the ADB also records fifty years of travelling to collect subscriptions and preaching at 87. The perpetual-motion work never produced a result, so impact is dual-edged. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.60 because the ADB carries most of the span, the 1919 report is his own claim, and the other entries repeat the ADB.

curiosity.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_griffiths, src_unaipon_rba, src_unaipon_awm | 1885-1944 | reference biography, historian's essay, institutional biographies] The ADB says his employer encouraged his interest in philosophy, science and music, that he read widely, and that in the 1920s he researched Egyptology at the South Australian Museum; Griffiths adds study of theology, mechanics, physics and languages, and the RBA and AWM record his work on aerodynamics and the boomerang. The interests are documented but mostly through one reference biography and institutional summaries that follow it. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.58 for source-family concentration on the ADB.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_britannica, src_unaipon_griffiths, src_unaipon_rba | 1902-1960s | reference biography, encyclopaedia, historian's essay, institutional biography] He worked as a bookkeeper and storeman, inventor, church organist, lecturer and preacher, newspaper and booklet writer, and compiler of Ngarrindjeri and other legends, and the sources agree that he moved between science, literature and public speaking. Much of this overlaps with his one role as the Aborigines' Friends' Association's travelling speaker, and the outputs in each field were uneven (patents lapsed, books published late). CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.58 because the biographical summaries are one family and the depth of the output differs by field.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_rba, src_unaipon_griffiths, src_unaipon_britannica | 1909-1914 | reference biography, institutional biography, historian's essay, encyclopaedia] The shearing handpiece converting circular into straight-line motion was patented by 1909 and he devised a centrifugal motor, a multi-radial wheel and a propulsion device, but sources disagree on the 1914 helicopter idea: the RBA and Griffiths credit a design drawn from the boomerang, while the ADB says he repeated predictions made by others. None of the sources describes how he came to the designs. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): top-risk row; lowered from 64 / 0.46 to 58 / 0.40 because the helicopter claim is contested and the 'Leonardo' label was press reputation.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_griffiths, src_unaipon_press1919, src_unaipon_eoas | 1912-1928 | reference biography, historian's essay, contemporary newspaper, reference entry] He led a deputation in 1912 asking for government control of Point McLeay Mission, began a lecturing campaign in 1919 to raise money for a patent, and from 1924 collected legends on a tour of southern and central Australia under a book contract; the ADB records him giving evidence to royal commissions and assisting the 1928-29 Bleakley inquiry. The acts are documented by four sources; his reasons come mainly from the biographers' reading.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_press1919, src_unaipon_rba, src_unaipon_awm | 1913-1934 | reference biography, contemporary newspaper, institutional biographies] The ADB says his rhetorical skills and his handling of the press made him the best-known Aboriginal man in Australia and that he influenced government policy through the 1920s and 1930s; he lectured in churches and cathedrals and to schools and learned societies, and a 1919 newspaper praised his fluency and platform manner. The influence on policy is asserted by the ADB without a specific decision traced to him. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.56 because the policy-influence claim rests on the ADB and the other entries repeat it.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_press1919, src_unaipon_awm, src_unaipon_rba | 1914-1950s | reference biography, contemporary newspaper, institutional biographies] He sold his own booklets while working for the Aborigines' Friends' Association, lectured to raise money for patent fees when no backer was found, and kept travelling on foot between towns despite being refused accommodation because of his race. Documented as circumstances; the sources do not describe how he solved particular problems. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.50 to 64 / 0.46 because hardship and the lack of backing are documented more clearly than his own methods.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_unaipon_awm, src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_rba | 1913-1934 | institutional profile, reference biography, institutional biography] The AWM quotes his stated wish that 'an enduring record of our customs, beliefs, and imaginings' be preserved and says he sought to improve Aboriginal education; the ADB and RBA record fifty years of lecturing and evidence to inquiries. The stated aim is his own words as quoted by one institution; the ADB also notes his public appeals for money were disapproved of by mission authorities. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 66 / 0.46 to 62 / 0.42 because the motive rests on a self-statement quoted by a single page.

aesthetic_sensitivity.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_griffiths, src_unaipon_rba | 1890-1924 | reference biography, historian's essay, institutional biography] He played the organ (the essay says Bach), memorised passages of Milton, and the ADB and Griffiths describe a prose style shaped by Milton, Bunyan, the Bible and the classics. These are documented tastes and a writing style; none of the sources assesses how he judged beauty.

adaptability.rationale: [src_unaipon_adb, src_unaipon_griffiths | 1885-1930s | reference biography, historian's essay] He moved between mission school, domestic service in Adelaide, bootmaking, a storeman's job, the mission store and a long travelling career, and Griffiths describes him writing for European readers in biblical and classical terms while holding to Ngarrindjeri traditions. The moves are documented but were partly forced by the lack of work for educated Aboriginal men at the mission, so the evidence for the trait is indirect.

portrait.source: Studio-style photographic print of David Unaipon (photographer not recorded) bound as the portrait in Volume 1 of the manuscript of 'Legendary Tales of Australian Aborigines' by David Unaipon, 1924-1925, Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales, call no. A 1929 (acquired with the Angus & Robertson publishing archive in 1933). The State Library itself published the same print on Flickr Commons as 'David Unaipon, 1925' (gelatin silver print, 501 x 640, 'taken sometime in 1925', licence line 'No known copyright restrictions'; the print carries the handwritten caption 'David Unaipon' under the image). The file used is the Wikimedia Commons copy of the State Library's digitisation of the same photograph (850 x 1072, cropped above the handwritten caption), used at its native size: not resized and not upscaled. Same photograph confirmed visually against the holder's Flickr copy.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: photograph taken in 1924-1925, before 1955, so its Australian copyright has expired (State Library of NSW 'About copyright' page: photographs taken before 1955 are out of copyright); the photographer is unrecorded; the holder's own Flickr Commons record states no known copyright restrictions. CAUTION: the State Library says it may restrict public-domain material that is culturally sensitive and may require cultural clearances for some Aboriginal material; the item-level catalogue record was behind a bot wall and could not be read.
portrait.attribution: Photographer unknown; portrait of David Unaipon, c. 1924-1925, from the manuscript of 'Legendary Tales of Australian Aborigines' (A 1929), Mitchell Library, State Library of New South Wales. Please acknowledge the State Library of New South Wales. Lifetime photograph of the sitter.
portrait.creator: Unknown photographer (print held by the State Library of New South Wales)
portrait.date: 1924-1925 (the holder's Flickr record says taken sometime in 1925; Commons says 1924)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (Stage B) / REPLACED: the lead's Cazneaux c. 1934 portrait (State Library of NSW ON 388/Box 061/Item 169) was dropped because its Commons page gives a date that contradicts itself (c. 1934 against 'published in The Home, 1 February 1925') and the holder item record is behind a bot wall (not bypassed). The replacement is the Stage B fallback route, upgraded: the portrait print bound into the 1924-1925 manuscript of Legendary Tales (A 1929), which the State Library itself published on Flickr Commons (page read; licence line 'No known copyright restrictions', 'taken sometime in 1925', handwritten caption 'David Unaipon' on the print). I viewed both the Flickr original (501 x 640) and the Commons copy of the same digitisation (850 x 1072, cropped above the caption) and they are the same photograph. HOLDER TERMS READ: State Library of NSW 'About copyright' (photographs taken before 1955 are out of copyright; the Library may still restrict public-domain material that is culturally sensitive) and 'Copyright and your responsibilities' (for some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander material users may be required to seek cultural clearances, with the Library's help). The item catalogue pages (collection.sl.nsw.gov.au and gather.sl.nsw.gov.au), the State Library of South Australia item (B 7326) and Trove/NLA pages were all behind bot walls and were not bypassed, so no item-level restriction statement could be read either way. CAVEAT FOR LEAD: ships on age plus the holder's own public Flickr Commons release; sitter is a deceased Aboriginal man with a public-figure profile (Australian $50 note), and a courtesy check with the State Library's Indigenous engagement staff or the Unaipon family is recommended. KIND likeness (lifetime photograph, photographer unrecorded). PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-24, Wikidata API) Q939297 label 'David Unaipon', description 'Indigenous Australian inventor and writer (1872-1967)', instance of human, born 28 September 1872, died 7 February 1967, citizenship Australia; no Korean label or Korean Wikipedia article (Korean display name is a transliteration, flagged). REGION western_europe (Australasian precedent Mawson/Rutherford/Wilkins). ERA 20th_century (patent 1909, writing from 1924). ATTRIBUTION: attributable (biography documented by dated patents, newspaper articles, publications, royal commission evidence and the surviving manuscript). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Philip Jones, Australian Dictionary of Biography entry. READ: ADB (full, via an Internet Archive copy of the online edition), Britannica (full), Billy Griffiths's Reading Australia essay (full), RBA banknotes entry, AWM profile, EOAS entry, a 1919 reprinted newspaper report (Press, Christchurch; Thames Star), and the abstract page of Kropinyeri and Bowery 2023 (full article not obtained). Wikipedia not used. Also read but not cited: National Portrait Gallery biography, State Library of South Australia guide, Quality Wool 'Offcuts' page (repeats shearing claims). NOT OPENED: the 2001 Muecke and Shoemaker introduction, Trimmer, Gower and Lock 2017, Gunson's 1999 interview, Simons's 'Nobody's hero' (1994), Jenkin, Jones's other work; Trove articles (bot wall). ZERO POLITICS: only behaviours are scored; his advocacy positions (1926 Aboriginal state proposal, 1934 call for Commonwealth control, 1938 disagreement over the Day of Mourning) and religious beliefs are not scored or carded as positions; his 1926 vagrancy arrest and his marriage are not used. CONTRADICTIONS AND LIMITS: shearing handpiece dated 1907 (EOAS) or 1909 (ADB, RBA, Britannica); number of patent applications is ten in all (ADB, AWM) or nineteen provisional patents (Griffiths); the 1914 helicopter idea is credited to him (RBA, Griffiths) but the ADB says he repeated others' predictions; whether Ramsay Smith 'commissioned' (ADB) or bought the manuscript from Angus & Robertson (Griffiths) differs; the 'Australia's Leonardo' label is press reputation. The claim that the shearing design became the standard handpiece is repeated by institutional pages and is not carded as fact; Kropinyeri and Bowery's article (abstract only) disputes how it was exploited. PERSPECTIVES: (1) reference biography (ADB, Jones); (2) literary-historian essay drawing on the 2001 edition's introduction (Griffiths); (3) contemporary press (1919, partly his own claims); (4) encyclopaedia (Britannica); (5) scholarly abstract on inventing under Protection restrictions (Kropinyeri and Bowery). INDEPENDENT BEHAVIOURAL FAMILIES: about four (Jones/ADB, with the RBA, AWM and EOAS entries derived from it; Muecke and Shoemaker via Griffiths; 1919 press; Kropinyeri and Bowery abstract, not used for rows). SPARSE PROFILE BY DESIGN: 10 rows, mostly 0.40-0.54 confidence. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards (1) first published Aboriginal author and the unacknowledged 1930 edition of his legends, (2) the shearing handpiece and the inventions that stalled, (3) fifty years as travelling speaker and witness to inquiries. SELF-CALIBRATION: see handback; nothing raised. HANDBACK70: see TGI-r70-scratch/handback/david-unaipon.json.
